lesson.title: Saber vs Conocer
lesson.subtitle: Knowing facts and skills (sé nadar, sé dónde está) vs knowing people and places (conozco Madrid, conozco a María)

hook.title: Two Ways of 'Knowing' That English Blurs Together
hook.content: In English, 'know' covers two completely different mental experiences: knowing a piece of information or a skill ('I know where it is, I know how to speak Spanish') vs being personally acquainted with a person or place ('I know María, I know Madrid'). Spanish gives each its own verb: **saber** (yo **sé** 'I know', tú sabes) for facts, information, and skills; and **conocer** (yo **conozco** 'I know/am familiar with', tú conoces) for people, places, and things you've met!

footnotes.title: What Happens When 'Saber' and 'Conocer' Enter the Preterite?
footnotes.content: In the preterite (dot in time), conocí a María means 'I met María for the first time', and supe la verdad means 'I found out the truth'!

pattern.title: Two Golden Shortcuts: 'Sé + Infinitive' (No *Cómo!) & 'Conozco a + Person'
pattern.content:
1) To say 'I know HOW to speak Spanish', Spanish uses **sé + bare infinitive** (Sé hablar español) — never insert *cómo!
2) When conocer is followed by a person, always include the personal 'a' (Conozco a María); when followed by a city, no 'a' (Conozco Madrid)!
pattern.trap_note: Notice the tilde on yo sé ('I know'): with an accent, sé means 'I know'; without an accent, se is the reflexive/indirect pronoun!

exercises.prompt: Match each English expression with its Spanish partner:

matching_pairs.english: to know (facts, information, how to do something)
I know (fact / skill: 1st sg. of saber)
to know / be familiar with (people, places)
I know / am acquainted with (1st sg. of conocer)

exercises.target_answer: saber, sé, conocer, conozco, sé dónde está, conozco Madrid
exercises.meaning: to know (facts, information, how to do something), I know (fact / skill: 1st sg. of saber), to know / be familiar with (people, places), I know / am acquainted with (1st sg. of conocer), I know where it is (fact/clause), I know Madrid (place)
exercises.explanation: saber (sé) = facts, clauses, and skills (+ infinitive); conocer (conozco) = people (with 'a') and places.

exercises.prompt: Spanish conocer ('to be familiar/acquainted with', from Latin cognōscere) shares its root with which formal English adjective meaning 'aware or having knowledge of'?
exercises.meaning: cognizant and recognize come from the exact same Latin root as conocer!
exercises.explanation: Latin cognōscere gave Spanish conocer and English cognizant, recognize, reconnaissance.

exercises.prompt: How do you say 'I know how to speak Spanish' in natural Spanish?
exercises.meaning: I know how to speak Spanish
exercises.explanation: saber + bare infinitive already means 'to know how to [verb]' — never add *cómo!

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'I know Madrid and I know your brother'
exercises.target_answer: Conozco Madrid y conozco a tu hermano
exercises.meaning: I know Madrid and I know your brother
exercises.explanation: Conozco Madrid (city = no 'a') y conozco a tu hermano (person = personal 'a'!).

exercises.idea: say that you don't know where the station is
cues: I don't know (fact/question clause → saber) → No sé
idea_parts: where the station is → dónde está la estación
exercises.target_answer: No sé dónde está la estación
exercises.meaning: I don't know where the station is
exercises.explanation: No sé dónde está la estación — notice sé ('I know') wears an accent mark to distinguish it from se ('himself/herself')!

diagnosis.cue: Before a question word or clause (qué, dónde, por qué, que...), always use saber (No sé dónde está).

summary.outcome: Distinguish saber (sé: facts, clauses, and skills + infinitive) from conocer (conozco: people and places).

use_example.german: Conozco Madrid, conozco a tu amigo y sé dónde está el restaurante.
use_example.english: I know Madrid, I know your friend, and I know where the restaurant is.

summary.takeaway: Facts, clauses, and infinitives take saber (sé); people and places take conocer (conozco).
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next ([24] Reflexives & Daily Life): see how me, te, se, nos turn actions back on the speaker in daily life.

twist.prompt: Assemble: 'Do you know where it is?'
twist.explanation: ¿Sabes dónde está? uses saber before a clause.

saber.english_meaning: to know (facts, information, how to do something; sé: I know)
saber.context_translation: I know how to speak Spanish.
saber.etymology_derivation: Used for facts, clauses, and skills (sé + bare infinitive, without 'cómo').

conocer.english_meaning: to know, be familiar with (people, places; conozco: I know)
conocer.shift_rule: 1st sg in -zco: conozco (takes personal 'a' before people!)
conocer.context_phrase: Conozco Madrid y conozco a tu hermano.
conocer.context_translation: I know Madrid and I know your brother.
conocer.etymology_derivation: Before a specific person, conhecer ALWAYS requires the personal 'a': conozco a María!

dónde.etymology_derivation: Latin dē + unde ('from where') → dónde. Carries written accent in questions.

qué.etymology_derivation: Latin quid → qué. Stressed in questions (accented qué), unstressed as conjunction (que).

hablar.english_meaning: to speak, to talk (hablo: I speak)
hablar.etymology_derivation: Latin fabulārī (to converse, tell stories — English fable and fabulous) shifted initial f- to silent h-: hablar!

hermano.context_phrase: Tengo un hermano y una hermana.
hermano.context_translation: I have a brother and a sister.
hermano.etymology_derivation: Latin germānus ('of the same seed/parents', English 'germane') lost its initial g- in Spanish: hermano!

ciudad.etymology_derivation: Latin cīvitātem ('citizenship, city') gives English 'city' and 'civic', and Spanish ciudad.

a.english_meaning: to, at (a + el = al; also personal 'a')
a.context_translation: I am going to the restaurant.
a.etymology_derivation: Fuses with masculine singular article el into al ('to the / at the').

cion.name: The -CIÓN Passport
cion.phonetic_rule: English -tion /-(e)ʃən/ becomes Spanish -ción /-ˈθjon/. Always stressed on the ó, and 100% feminine (la).
cion.historical_linguistics: Descends from Latin third-declension abstract nouns in -tiō (accusative -tiōnem). English borrowed thousands via French; Spanish evolved -ción directly.
cion.philological_note: Because every single -ción noun is feminine, this family hands you grammatical gender for thousands of words without memorization.

dad.name: The -DAD Quality Bridge
dad.phonetic_rule: English abstract nouns in -ty correspond to Spanish -dad /-ˈdað/. 100% feminine (la).
dad.historical_linguistics: From Latin abstract quality nouns in -tās, accusative -tātem. Spanish lenited the intervocalic dental stop to -dad.
dad.philological_note: City (ciudad), reality (realidad), university (universidad). The ending guarantees feminine gender.

mente.name: The -MENTE Adverb Engine
mente.phonetic_rule: Feminine adjective + -mente /-ˈmente/ forms adverbs corresponding to English -ly.
mente.historical_linguistics: Originates from the Latin ablative phrase [adjective] mente ('with a ... mind'). Because mens is feminine in Latin, Spanish preserves the feminine adjective stem.
mente.philological_note: Notice how Spanish preserves the feminine form: exactamente (not exactomente). If the base adjective carries a tilde, it keeps it: fácilmente.

ar_engine.name: The -ar Verb Factory
ar_engine.phonetic_rule: English Latinate nouns in -ation correspond to Spanish first-conjugation infinitives in -ar /-ˈaɾ/.
ar_engine.historical_linguistics: Latin first-conjugation verbs in -āre. English borrowed the noun form; Spanish kept the verb stem alive.
ar_engine.philological_note: The 'celebrar trap': strip the entire -ation before attaching -ar. Celebración → celebrar (not celebratar).

ico.name: The -ICO Bridge
ico.phonetic_rule: English adjectives in -ic / -ical correspond to Spanish -ico /-iko/ (masculine) / -ica (feminine). Always carries a written accent on the antepenultimate syllable.
ico.historical_linguistics: Greek -ikos passed through Latin -icus. In Spanish, these are palabras esdrújulas and must be written with a tilde.
ico.philological_note: Mágico, público, básico, económico, romántico. The tilde tells your voice exactly where to jump.

al.name: The -AL Invariable Passport
al.phonetic_rule: English adjectives ending in -al match Spanish -al /-ˈal/ with identical spelling and gender-invariable singular form.
al.historical_linguistics: Latin adjectival suffix -ālis ('pertaining to'). Both languages kept the spelling; Spanish stresses the final syllable.
al.philological_note: El plan natural, la idea natural: no gender change in the singular.

f_to_h.name: Latin F- ➔ Silent H-
f_to_h.phonetic_rule: Latin initial f- weakened into an aspiration and became completely silent h- in Spanish, while English kept the Latin f- cognate.
f_to_h.historical_linguistics: Castilian contact with Basque/Cantabrian substrate languages lacking initial /f/ caused Latin /f-/ to weaken into silent h-.
f_to_h.philological_note: Hacer ↔ fact/manufacture; hijo ↔ filial; hierro ↔ ferrous; horno ↔ furnace. When you see a silent h-, think f.

ct_to_ch.name: Latin -CT- ➔ Spanish -CH-
ct_to_ch.phonetic_rule: Latin medial -ct- palatalized into Spanish -ch- /-tʃ-, while English kept the learned Latin -ct- form.
ct_to_ch.historical_linguistics: The velar stop /k/ vocalized into a palatal glide [j] which then fused with the dental /t/ into the affricate /tʃ/.
ct_to_ch.philological_note: Noctem ➔ noche (nocturnal); lactem ➔ leche (lactose); factum ➔ hecho (fact); octō ➔ ocho (octave).

pl_cl_fl_to_ll.name: Latin PL-/CL-/FL- ➔ Spanish LL-
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.phonetic_rule: Latin initial consonant clusters pl-, cl-, fl- palatalized into Spanish ll- /ʎ/ (or /ʝ/).
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.historical_linguistics: The initial stop or fricative conditioned progressive palatalization of the liquid /l/ in Western Iberian Vulgar Latin.
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.philological_note: Clāmāre ➔ llamar (claim/clamor); clāvis ➔ llave (clef/clavicle); pluvia ➔ lluvia (pluvial); plēnus ➔ lleno (plenty).
